name: Weight on other planets
seoTitle: Weight on other planets Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Weight on other planets: work out mercury from the venus. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Weight on other planets calculator returns mercury from the field on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Weight on other planets calculator work?
sections.html:
The Weight on other planets calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mercury in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the venus.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html: • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the Weight on other planets calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Mercury=(19 ÷ 50) × your weight on Earth
Your weight on Earth=(100 ÷ 91) × venus
Mars=(19 ÷ 50) × your weight on Earth
Jupiter=(117 ÷ 50) × your weight on Earth
Your weight on Earth=(50 ÷ 53) × saturn
Uranus=(23 ÷ 25) × your weight on Earth

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Your weight on Earth = 10 kg. The calculator returns Mercury = 4 kg, Venus = 9 kg, Mars = 4 kg and Jupiter = 23 kg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mercury = 4 kg, Venus = 9 kg, Mars = 4 kg and Jupiter = 23 kg should be roughly the size you expected from Your weight on Earth = 10 kg.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Weight on other planets calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the venus — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Weight on other planets calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mercury, derived from the venus. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Weight on other planets calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the venus, which is a single field. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your weight on Earth in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your weight on Earth opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mercury = 4 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Weight on other planets calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
